newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Reformer Nemtsov dreams of making Russians happy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Reformer Nemtsov dreams of making Russians happy.

text.p: Boris Nemtsov, the young reformer summoned from the provinces by President Boris Yeltsin to revive reforms, wants to go down in history as a man who made life better for ordinary Russians.

That is one of the goals the new first deputy prime minister sets in a book which reveals deep admiration for Yeltsin, whom he calls a tsar, an intense desire to win and a realisation that he will not be forgiven if he fails.

"My success will be absolute when people start living better and, if my investment in this success is visible, when people say 'it was so-an-so in the Nemtsov times and now it is different'," 37-year-old Nemtsov writes in "The Provincial".

The book, written before the boyish-looking Nemtsov took up his Kremlin post last month, is about to hit Russian bookstores. In it, he shares his views on himself, society and leading Russian and foreign figures.

Nemtsov, former governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region about 350 km (220 miles) east of Moscow, was named one of two first deputies to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin under a sweeping reshuffle giving the go-ahead for major changes.

"A desire to win is definitely one of my qualities, though I can't say I want to win at any cost...I win quite often," he wrote. "Sometimes it feels that results are unpredictable, but then life shows that I have won."
UNOFFICIAL HEIR?
Some analysts speculate that Yeltsin, 66, may have chosen Nemtsov as his unofficial heir and brought him to Moscow to train him until his own term as president ends.
Nemtsov recalls in the book how Yeltsin once told him during a visit to Nizhny Novgorod that he was politically mature enough to become the next president of Russia.
"Yeltsin offered me the presidency. That was a joke of course...but this joke had a huge echo," he wrote.
Nemtsov speaks of himself as a political kamikaze, referring to the Japanese pilots who went on missions knowing they would die.
"Russia is a cruel country. It does not pardon you even for the good things you did for it. People do not thank you here," he wrote.
Nemtsov says he enjoys fame but hates the task of forcing people to do things. He loathes Moscow's behind-the-scenes political fights.

His task in his new post could require a lot of force. He is in charge of a drive to put powerful monopolies under tight government control and many experts say he is behind a new Yeltsin crusade against corruption by state officials.
"Oh, yes, they steal," Nemtsov writes in the book, where he also offers some cures for the centuries-old disease.
"It is hard to make an injection against stealing...regular re-election is one of them, the other is private property -- a mighty means against stealing."

One of his first steps as first deputy prime minister was a pledge to drive foreign cars out of the Kremlin car pool and to make officials ride Russian-made cars from his home town of Nizhny Novgorod.
He says he himself likes Mitsubishi Pajero four-wheel-drive vehicles, but plans to buy a Russian Volga.
CHARACTER ANALYSES

The book also presents Nemtsov's views on political leaders and celebrities, ranging from politicians such as Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton to musician Mstislav Rostroprovich and actor Richard Gere.
"Yeltsin is a real Russian tsar -- reckless, capable of going on a spree, courageous and seldom shy. As opposed to ugly Russian tsars Yeltsin is a kind tsar," Nemtsov writes.
"He is a rebel in his soul, you can expect all kinds of things form him."
Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher also won Nemtsov's admiration.

"She is a real politician with all the pluses and minuses...Russia needs someone like Thatcher, someone who knows what to do, how to do it, patriotically minded and loyal enough to the rest of the world."
Nemtsov says another popular Russian politician, liberal economist Grigory Yavlinsky, could be a good leader for Russia.
"It would not harm Russia if he were a prime minister or a president. He is an economically-educated person, who cannot take any crazy decision which would make people suffer," he wrote.
He also views the other newly-appointed first deputy prime minister, Anatoly Chubais, as one of Russia's most talented politicians.

Nemtsov describes law-and-order general Alexander Lebed as an educated, colourful and charismatic politician, but says he needs to formulate his economic views to become a strong condender for the presidency.
